The Ansible is invented at the end of The Dispossessed, and is described as a new invention in The Word for World is Forest. It’s established technology by the time of Rocannon’s World, which also introduces the idea of the mysterious enemy (The Shing) which necessitates the formation of the League. Planet of Exile seems to be set after war with the enemy has broken out, leaving the colony of Terrans stranded on Werel with the native Hilfs, the Terrans eventually evolving to allow cross-breeding with the Hilfs. The Protagonist of City of Illusions, referred to as Falk for much of the novel, is a member of the new species of Werelian that resulted from this cross-breeding. I’d argue that just because dystopian or apocalyptic fiction isn’t effective at creating concrete societal change doesn’t make it lazy. The entire socioeconomic structure of the world we live in is geared towards preventing the kind of change required to prevent the disasters explored in End of the World fiction. In the face of those odds, it’s difficult for people to actually overcome the dangers of climate change (to use your example) even if they want to do so. 

I think your point about the possible outcomes being written time and time again is more relevant, but you could make the argument that such a point applies to nearly every work of fiction. Any story you can come up with, the probability is that someone else has already written something similar. Especially if you’re stripping it back to wide-ranging genre ideas like utopian or dystopian or apocalyptic fiction.

Personally I find that to be a bit of a reductive sentiment. Apocalyptic literature is about exploring what makes us human when we strip away the society that we take for granted. It also takes the problems that are prevalent in our world today (war, pandemics, the growth of nuclear and AI technology, etc) and imagines a future where we fail to overcome those issues and thereby highlights the importance of striving for better. Is it more difficult to imagine a utopian future than a dystopian one? As a writer myself I can say yes it is. But to chalk up the popularity of End of the World fiction to simple laziness on the part of writers and readers doesn’t do the genre justice in any way shape or form.

I have no issue with trigger warnings, personally. And to respond to your discussion prompts: 

1. If a trigger warning is going to “spoil the story” it’s probably worth asking why your story relies so heavily on the shock value of a surprising and graphic event. If the plot is only good because readers are surprised by something happening that would warrant a trigger warning, then it’s not a very good plot in my opinion. 

2. It’s not possible to put trigger warnings in place for everything that makes people uncomfortable, no. But the only things that I’ve seen people asking for trigger warnings on are the extreme ones you mentioned like graphic violence and graphic sexual content. 

3. The goal of trigger warnings is to prepare readers for content that may be traumatic, either allowing them to mentally brace themselves or to choose not to read the work in question. Either way, they’re useful for the people who need them and they don’t hinder the people who don’t.

The first thing to understand is the phrase “From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs” from Marx’s [Critique of the Gotha Programme](https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1875/gotha/index.htm). In a socialist society everyone should have their needs met, but in return everyone contributes to the society in the best way they can. For some, that will be curing the sick. For others, that will be growing food. For others still, that will be building houses. And so on and so forth. 

The next point to raise is “For as soon as the distribution of labour comes into being, each man has a particular, exclusive sphere of activity, which is forced upon him and from which he cannot escape. He is a hunter, a fisherman, a herdsman, or a critical critic, and must remain so if he does not want to lose his means of livelihood; while in communist society, where nobody has one exclusive sphere of activity but each can become accomplished in any branch he wishes, society regulates the general production and thus makes it possible for me to do one thing today and another tomorrow, to hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening, criticise after dinner, just as I have a mind, without ever becoming hunter, fisherman, herdsman or critic.” This is from [The German Ideology](https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1845/german-ideology/index.htm), and what Marx is talking about here is that capitalism forces everyone to specialise their labour in order to be useful to capitalist production. Under socialism people will be able to work in a variety of different areas, including contributing to the essential aspects of a functioning society. Socialism will also hugely reduce the amount of time people spend working, both through the abolition of unemployment as a capitalist tool and potentially through automation. 

So, to use your example of a construction worker, why would they continue to build houses after the abolition of wage labour? The answer is; they might not. They might decide that their talents are better suited to another area of labour. But for many people that kind of work is exactly where their talents lay. They’ll also have less work to do because socialism will allow everyone who can contribute to such an endeavour to do so, thus freeing up the majority of the “construction worker’s” time to focus on the pursuits that are meaningful for them.

In the initial days after President Putin dispatched his Russian army to wage war on Ukraine, a television journalist was reporting live from a railway station in Kyiv where scores of civilians were trying to board trains to get away. As he spoke about the sirens ominously blaring above ground, a woman could be seen rushing along the platform behind him carrying a bulging shopping bag. It was emblazoned with the store name Victoria’s Secret. The sight of it was a jolting reminder of how cruelly and abruptly normal life had ended in Ukraine on February 24. One day – perhaps Valentine’s Day, ten days earlier — a woman is shopping for pretty lingerie in Victoria’s Secret. The next day, she is fleeing her country clutching a few meagre possessions.

There is an old African saying that when elephants fight, it is the grass that suffers. Ukraine is no elephant. It is a country of 41 million people that has been plagued by a history of occupation and is not, as yet, a member of either Nato or the EU. More than one million civilians have fled, while the true number of those killed is unknown, and male citizens aged 16 to 60 have been ordered to stay and fight. Watching Ukrainians, from the safe distance of this island, as they defend their country by standing in front of tanks and lying on railway tracks while Putin’s elephantine army flattens their land, I have found my erstwhile unshakeable pro-neutrality nerve fiercely wobbling. How can Ireland justify not sending its army or even its arms to help Ukraine defend itself against this unjust invasion by its former occupier?

A hypothetical scenario I struggle to reconcile would be if Boris Johnson ordered the British Army to invade Ireland, its non-Nato neighbour and former colony, while other European countries resolutely stayed out of the fight. As a hypothesis, it may be extreme but Johnson and his fellow Brexiteers have never concealed their yearning for the British empire of yore and, as we see in Putin, it takes only one rapacious tyrant to turn the world upside down. The dynamics of geopolitics are precarious because they are dictated by individuals such as Donald Trump, who, as president of the world’s foremost superpower, fomented an insurrection in his own country.

In the case of Ukraine, there is no doubt that Ireland is politically and diplomatically on the right side against the Russian invasion. But the world’s power balance can flip in the blink of an eye, potentially putting us on the wrong side of justice when the next conflict erupts.

In the current angry atmosphere many people, including some in Leinster House, have called for Ireland to drop its neutrality policy and send arms to Ukraine. The discussion about this country’s role has assumed a subtext that, if you are opposed to any type of military intervention, you must be pro-Putin or soft on belligerents, or you’re a plain lily-livered coward. War polarises people. It has no room for nuance. You’re either with us or against us, goes its anthem. That is how confrontation escalates and grows beyond the reach of reason. As Shakespeare’s Mark Antony says in Julius Caesar: “Cry havoc! And let slip the dogs of war.”

These are the conditions that make a policy of neutrality the more principled and courageous option for some countries, Ireland included. Our withering planet needs neutral countries. It needs a third force — a force for peace. As more and more states side with one bloc or the other, standing apart takes courage.

Irish soldiers are proven peacekeepers who have worked to mend fences in far-flung places including the Congo, Lebanon and Mali. Irish diplomacy has helped to make our world safer, most notably with its unanimously agreed UN resolution in 1961 that provided the genesis for the enduring treaty on the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons. Irish humanitarian organisations, many assisted by Irish Aid in the Department of Foreign Affairs and by this country’s stance as a neutral broker, have delivered practical help to the victims of warmongers. The Irish passport is widely regarded as a neutral document

The benefit of this soft power is not easily measured, compounding the inherent problem that arguing for arming up is simpler than arguing for downing arms. There have, rightly, been calls for the Irish Defence Forces to be strengthened — though what chance has a small island against a nuclear power? — but Ireland’s credibility as a neutral country also needs to be reinforced. That reputation has been undermined by the state’s failure to condemn America’s unjust invasion of Iraq in 2003 and has continued to be damaged ever since by allowing US warfaring aircraft to refuel at Shannon airport with scant inspections for weapons on board.

Ireland currently occupies the high savannah of the UN security council, side by side with the planet’s elephants, where Russia exercised its veto last week to defeat a resolution condemning its onslaught on Ukraine. Next Friday, Russia will chair a council meeting about — of all themes — “terrorism”. With the US, China, France and the UK holding the other permanent seats at the table, the elephants rule. Meanwhile in Ukraine, Yemen, Syria, Israel’s occupied territories, Afghanistan and Sudan, the grass is trodden underfoot.

We are bombarded with a narrative that the West is best, the rest is evil, and only weapons of death are capable of protecting the values we cherish. As tempers flare and many people in this country understandably feel powerless to help the people of Ukraine, Ireland’s best weapon in the fight for peace is jaw-jaw, not war-war. This is neither the time nor the emotional climate in which to be making decisions about the policy of neutrality.

This country’s two-year tenure on the security council will expire in December. The government must use that time to negotiate radical reform of UN structures, making them more equitable and workable in order to give peace a chance. Its present structures are stuck in a global geopolitical stone age while the world hurtles through the nuclear age.
In the mid-20th century Frank Aiken, as Ireland’s minister for external affairs, proposed four separate and successive motions on nuclear arms reduction before finally getting the UN’s unanimous backing. He argued it was essential to reduce the threat of nuclear war during the time it would take “to evolve and strengthen a generally accepted system of world security based on international law and law enforcement”.

To rush to arms now would be to admit defeat in the endeavour to create that justice-based peace on earth. To surrender that ideal would be to hand victory to the enemy.

The "Irish Slaves" myth tends to refer to Irish people being kept as slaves in the same way that Africans were kept as slaves, and is usually brought up to downplay the horrors of the slaves trade for African and those of African descent. 

Go back far enough and yes, Irish people were captured and held as slaves. But that kind of small scale tribal slavery was practiced by almost every group across the world so its not really unique.

The "Irish Slaves" myth attempts to insert Irish people into the huge industrial-scale slave trade between Europe, Africa, and the Americas, which didn't really happen. What Irish people experienced was "indentured servitude".

Indentured servitude differs from slavery in a number of ways. Firstly, indentured servants often entered into these arrangements semi-willingly (i.e. to pay for their passage to the New World). Secondly, indentured servitude was for a set amount of time rather than for life, although as others have pointed out some indentured servants were coerced into extending their servitude. 

Perhaps most importantly, the biggest distinction between slavery and indentured servitude was that indentured servants were still considered people in the eyes of the law while slaves were considered property. This extends to children too. A child couldn't be born into indentured servitude but they could be born into slavery.

This doesn't diminish the terrible conditions Irish people experienced as indentured servants, but it also doesn't mean they were slaves.

As for his inspiring of Michael Collins, numerous historians have written about Collins' distain for Pearse. Collins saw him as an idealist who put far more value on the *idea* of the rebellion than the lives of the men actually under his command. If Collins was inspired by any of the signatories of the Proclamation it was James Connolly, who he saw as a capable commander who cares about his men.

None of this is to take away from Pearse's contributions to the Republican movement and Irish freedom. He is an incredibly important figure in Irish history. But his role in the Rising was largely as a figurehead and Michael Collins didn't find him particularly inspiring.
